SPTestMetricsChart.description: Suite Health page charts. A top-level map keyed by chart name (no data wrapper).

SPTestBaseInfo.description: Identifying header info for one test in the Test Health detail view. Flat object, no data wrapper.

name.description: Test display name; empty string when the hash matches nothing in the window.

combinations.description: OS/browser/device environment combinations the test ran on.

browser.description: Formatted browser descriptor, with a nested `device` field.

SPTestEnvironmentBreakdown.description: Per-environment stability breakdown for one test. A BARE JSON array (no object wrapper).

TestRunDetailResponse.description: Full detail of a single test run.

TestRunDetailMapResponse.description: A MAP keyed by test run id; each value is that run's detail ({ testCode, testMetadata }). Empty object when nothing matched — not an error.

BuildInsightsResponse.description: Build-level insights surrounding a test run.

BuildTestRunListingResponse.description: A build's test runs as a nested suite/folder/test hierarchy with deep-link URLs, plus pagination. Envelope varies by account flag: newer accounts carry workflowStatusAggregate + isManuallyOverridden, older ones statusAggregate.

hierarchy.description: Nested nodes (suites/folders/tests). Each node has details, children, and an external deep-link URL. On freemium/source-fenced builds analysis keys are stripped from node details.

statusAggregate.description: Present on the older envelope only.

workflowStatusAggregate.description: Present on the newer envelope only.

isManuallyOverridden.description: Present on the newer envelope only.

nextPage.description: Opaque base64 cursor; echo back as next_page.

TestRunAttachmentUrlsResponse.description: A page of presigned attachment/screenshot URLs for one test run.

BuildTestRunsWithAttachmentsResponse.description: Trimmed test-run rows that have attachments/screenshots, with a numeric cursor.

next_cursor.description: Numeric cursor; null on the last page. Pass back as `cursor`.

PlainTextConfirmation.description: A fixed plain-text success string (e.g. 'Auto unmute cancelled successfully!'). Not JSON.

BugReportDraftResponse.description: Pre-filled bug-report draft composed from a failed run. Read-only; not a stored bug.

testDetails.description: Composed test hierarchy/description text for the ticket body.

logStruct.description: Image/log attachment references; empty when the run has no screenshots.

aiRca.description: AI RCA snippet; absent when no RCA is available.

LinkBugToTestRunResponse.description: Result of linking a filed bug to a run. 200 carries the created integration id; a 204 (no body) means the bug key was already tracked.

id.description: Created integration id; null if none was recorded.

FlatTestRunListingResponse.description: Flat list of a build's test runs with search_after pagination.

searchAfter.description: Cursor to pass back as searchAfter for the next page.

BuildAIFailuresResponse.description: Build-level AI failure analysis: failure themes and workflows, sorted by failure share. Serialized from AIFailuresResponse; trialQuota is omitted (NON_NULL) unless the account is on the build-level trial.

buildThemes.description: Failure themes, sorted by testPercentage descending.

buildFailureThemeId.description: Integer id used to drill into this theme's test runs.

testPercentage.description: Share of failures as a string (may include a % sign).

ci_trigger.title: CI trigger (and CI trigger secret)
ci_trigger.description: A saved CI/CD webhook config (Jenkins, GitLab, custom) that Test Reporting can fire to start a build, plus the named secrets it references.
ci_trigger.id_convention: UUID — both triggers and secrets are addressed by their `uuid`; the integer DB id is never exposed. Discover ids through the list calls.
key_facts: Two kinds of record live here: the CI trigger (the saved webhook configuration) and the CI trigger secret (a named credential). A trigger references a secret by writing the secret's name in square brackets, e.g. [JENKINS_TOKEN], inside the trigger's URL, headers or body.
Secret names must be UPPER_SNAKE_CASE: start with a capital letter, then only capitals, digits and underscores. A lowercase, hyphenated or leading-digit name is rejected.
Stored credentials and secret values are only Base64-obfuscated at rest, not encrypted (acknowledged in a code comment) — treat them as recoverable plaintext, not protected secrets.
Reads never return secret material: a trigger read reports only whether a Jenkins/auth token is set, and a secret read never carries its value.

The resolve/preview operation is the one deliberate exception and is a credential-disclosure surface: it returns the decoded plaintext of every secret a trigger references to anyone who can see the trigger, and returns the trigger's own stored Jenkins/auth tokens in plaintext to the trigger's owner.

Visibility is your own records plus any marked shared, scoped to your group. A shared trigger can be fired and resolved by any group member, using the owner's stored credentials, but only the owner can edit or delete it.
Firing a trigger makes a real outbound HTTP call to the customer-configured CI URL and starts a build — it cannot be undone, and a disabled trigger is refused.
Neither triggers nor secrets keep any version history: an overwritten field cannot be restored, so edits are irreversible in content even though the record survives.
Deleting a trigger or a secret is permanent. A secret that is still referenced by any trigger in the group cannot be deleted until the reference is removed.
Renaming a secret does not rewrite the triggers that referenced its old name — those bracketed placeholders silently stop resolving (they then expand to empty at fire time).
A new trigger is created enabled.
Names are unique per record within a group and user; creating or renaming to a name already in use is rejected as a duplicate.
Every create, update, delete, execute and resolve is blocked in the demo-sandbox environment; plain reads still work there.

integration.title: Integration & notification preference
integration.description: A signed-in user's connection to a third-party tool (Jira, Slack, CI) or their email-notification settings, stored per user.
integration.id_convention: Addressed in the path by a fixed tool name (an IntegrationEnum value such as JIRA, SLACK, JENKINS), matched case-insensitively; there is no numeric integration id. Individual notification rules carry integer ids that must be discovered by reading the per-project email-preference detail first.

relations.via: email notification rules are scoped per project id

key_facts: Integrations are stored per user, not per group: connecting or disconnecting a tool changes only the signed-in user's setup, and other teammates in the same org keep their own connections.

A stored integration holds a username and an auth token; the token is only base64-encoded at rest, never encrypted, and reading the integration back returns the token decoded to plaintext, so the read result is a secret.

An integration is addressed by a fixed tool name (Jira, Slack, Jenkins, Azure DevOps, Linear, GitHub Actions, CircleCI, GitLab CI, and the per-type email notifications); an unrecognised name is rejected as not found.
Connecting a tool that is already connected is refused; change the existing connection instead of connecting a second time.
Disconnecting a tool deletes its stored credential outright: there is no undo and the credential must be entered again to reconnect.

Email-notification settings exist in several generations that are NOT interchangeable: one keys everything by notification-type name (daily summary, build insights, alerts, test failure), an older one by the raw email-type name, and the newest is organised per project around a notifier; read settings back in the same generation you intend to write.
The integration health score is an org-wide (group) value behind a feature flag; when the flag is off for the org the score reads as inaccessible rather than empty.
Marking a score category not-applicable is limited to org admins or owners or a Product Admin, and it needs the score row to already exist, so the score must be read once before it can be edited.
Bulk toggling notification rules consumes integer rule ids that only come from reading the per-project notification detail, so that detail must be read before the toggle write.
Saving any preference is a silent no-op in the demo-sandbox environment: it reports success without changing anything.

notification.title: Notification (and notifier)
notification.description: A project's alerting config: recipients (email/Slack notifiers) and their daily-summary, build-insight and alert subscriptions.
notification.id_convention: A notifier id is a plain integer, discovered from the project's recipient list (there is no prefixed identifier). The per-alert and per-build-name mapping ids used when toggling a single subscription are also plain integers, found by reading one notifier's configuration first.

relations.via: scoped to one project
a notifier subscribes to a project's alerts by alert id
build-insight subscriptions are keyed by build name

key_facts: Every project has two independent notifier channels, email and Slack, and almost every read and write acts on ONE channel that you must name; the same project can have a completely different set of email recipients and Slack recipients.

Reading the recipient list or a single recipient's configuration needs only project read access; every change to recipients or subscriptions needs the project's notification-settings permission, and a change to a recipient owned by another group is refused.

Editing one recipient's subscriptions is a FULL REPLACE, not a patch: subscriptions you omit are removed, and there is no version history, so a prior configuration cannot be restored once overwritten.
Bulk enabling or disabling of subscriptions is applied one entry at a time with no overall transaction, so a single bad entry aborts partway and leaves the earlier entries already changed.

A Test Management caller addresses a project by its Test Management project id, which is translated to the underlying observability project id; an id with no mapping reads as project-not-found rather than empty.
In a recipient-list summary, a subscription count of -1 is a sentinel meaning the recipient is subscribed to all builds or all alerts, not a real count.

The daily-summary email content builders select builds themselves (the latest few in a time window) unless you hand them explicit build ids; the fully enriched daily report also merges several aggregations plus best-effort AI summaries that are silently dropped when they fail, so those fields can be absent.
Two of the notification settings operations address the project by its normalised NAME instead of its numeric id.

Validating typed-in recipient email addresses is not a side-effect-free lookup: for each address that resolves to an in-group user it also provisions that user's email-integration records if they do not exist yet.
The home notification feed is capped to roughly the first fifty entries however deep you page, and when the feature is switched off for the group it returns an empty payload rather than an error.

Sending a test Slack notification posts a fixed sample message to the channel and stores nothing; only the daily-summary, build-insight and alert sample types are supported and it is suppressed in the demo-sandbox environment.

public_link.title: Public link & status badge
public_link.description: Anonymous share credentials: public-link tokens for dashboards and project report pages, plus signed keys for build-status badges.
public_link.id_convention: A public-link token is an opaque server-generated string, discovered only by calling the get-token operation for a dashboard or project (there is no list). A status-badge key is a signed JWT minted on demand. Dashboards are addressed by UUID; projects by their TestHub project id.

relations.via: one token per dashboard (page type CUSTOM_DASHBOARD)
one token per (project, page type)

key_facts: Two kinds of share credential live here: a public-link token that unlocks a dashboard or a project report page for anyone with the URL, and a status-badge key (a signed JWT) that exposes one build's high-level status for embedding.

Asking for a token is itself what starts sharing: the fetch creates the token on first request and leaves it enabled. There is no separate create step, so a plain read has a side effect the first time.
The public-link setting defaults to OFF. A dashboard or project whose setting has never been touched reads as not shared rather than as an error.

Turning sharing off immediately breaks every share URL already handed out and clears the token's cached validation, so revocation takes effect at once. Turning it back on reactivates the SAME token, so it is reversible but disruptive; there is no separate undo.

A project token is scoped to a single report page type (build insights, test runs, test health, unique errors or testing trends). Custom dashboards are a distinct page type reached only through the dashboard token operation.
A status-badge key is a bearer credential: once minted it cannot be revoked or listed, it exposes that build's status to anyone holding it, and it is refused for free-plan users.
Projects are named here by their TestHub project id, which is not the same as the observability project id.

quality_gate.title: Quality gate (and quality profile)
quality_gate.description: A pass/fail policy on a build, made of quality profiles: named rule sets (thresholds on status, flakiness, failure categories, etc.) scop...
quality_gate.id_convention: A quality profile is addressed by its UUID (path `profile_id`/`profileUuid`); a project by its normalised name; a build by its UUID. There are no integer ids on these routes. The one built-in default profile has a fixed UUID and behaves specially.

relations.via: profiles are mapped to a project; project attributes hold the feature enabled/override switches
the gate is evaluated per build; results are read from the parent build for a split build's child

key_facts: Editing a quality profile does NOT change it in place: it writes a new version and mints a NEW UUID, which the response returns. The UUID you edited stops resolving afterwards, so always carry the returned UUID forward. (The source inventory's claim that the UUID is stable is wrong.)
Deleting a quality profile is not reversible through the API. The profile is retired and its project mapping removed; there is no restore call, so treat it as permanent.

The one built-in default profile can be neither edited nor deleted (attempts are rejected). Enabling or disabling a default profile applies only to the one project, whereas enabling or disabling a custom profile applies across every project it is attached to.

There are two separate switches: one turns Quality Gates on or off for a whole project (and sets whether a failed gate also marks the build failed), the other enables or disables a single profile. They are different operations even though they share a name internally.

On the create and edit body the two fields go on the wire as `isGlobalProfile` and `applicableBuilds`; the internal names `isRootProfile` and `buildFilters` are not accepted and, if sent, are dropped and then fail the required-field check.
A profile must carry between 1 and 20 rules, and every rule must include a client-generated UUID `id`; a rule with an out-of-range test status, threshold, smart tag or alert level is rejected.

Quality gate evaluation runs asynchronously after a build finishes, so a build's gate result reads back as 'running'/pending until it completes and a CI check must poll rather than assume a single call is final.
A profile's ruleStatus ('pass' vs 'fail') decides how the per-profile outcome is computed: 'pass' means every rule must hold, 'fail' means none may hold.

Quality Gates is a plan-gated feature: when the plan lacks it, profile reads and writes are refused as feature-inaccessible, which is a plan gap and not a missing profile. The project-level on/off switch and the build-page result reads skip that plan check.
For a split build's child, gate results are read from the parent build, so a child on its own can look like it has no results.
Failure-category rules are enriched with the project's human display names only on the single-profile detail reads, not on the list or settings reads.
A profile can only be deleted from the group that owns it; deleting one that belongs to another group is refused.

testing_trends.title: Testing Trends
testing_trends.description: Aggregated quality-trend cards for a project - flakiness, stability, performance, failures and coverage over a time window.
testing_trends.id_convention: Not addressed by its own id. Scoped by the project's normalised name in the path and narrowed by build name. Chart and leaderboard rows are addressed by build name as the identifier, or by the literal "all" for the project-wide series.

relations.via: buildName filter / row identifier

key_facts: Every card is scoped to one project and a time window given as two epoch-millisecond bounds. When a bound is omitted it defaults to the plan's data-retention window, so a call with no window still returns the retention window's data.

The window is silently clamped to the plan's data retention: asking for data older than the plan retains returns retention-bounded results with no error and nothing in the body to say the window was narrowed.
Time-bucket granularity (hour / day / week) is chosen automatically from the width of the window, so the series interval changes as the window widens; the caller cannot set it.
The flakiness, new-failures and always-failing cards are plan-feature-gated: on a plan without that widget the call is refused with a 403, it does not return empty data.

Build frequency is the one card that requires both window bounds and does NOT clamp them to retention; its counts come from the relational build store rather than the analytics index, so they can differ slightly from the other cards.
Opening the recent-runs picker records the project as subscribed for the calling user - a persisted user preference, so that read has a lasting side effect.
Any card can be narrowed to a single build by its build name; the leaderboards and charts address a specific build by that name, or use the literal "all" for the project-wide series.
Leaderboards return a fixed number of builds per page and expose only a zero-based page number, not a page size; a hasNext flag in the response tells you whether to fetch the next page.
The always-failing card also records the trends view in the calling user's recently-viewed list for non-superusers, a minor convenience side effect that does not change any test data.
Test-growth counts distinct test cases (suite size) over the window, not test executions; test-executions counts how many tests ran. They answer different questions despite looking similar.

user_team.title: User & team (group membership)
user_team.description: People in a BrowserStack group (and the teams that group them) as Test Observability sees them, for pickers, invites, access and identity...
user_team.id_convention: Users are the BrowserStack integer user id; teams are the BrowserStack integer team id. Discover both through the group / sub-group user and team listings rather than guessing them.

relations.via: users are grouped into teams and sub-groups

key_facts: Users and teams here are BrowserStack-account objects: a user's id is their BrowserStack account id and a team's id is a BrowserStack team id — not the Test-Management user/team ids used elsewhere in the product.
The group and sub-group are always taken from the authenticated session, never passed in — you can only list the caller's own group's people, not an arbitrary group's.
A listed user record carries only id, email and full name; there is no richer profile available through this surface.
When a report is opened through a public share link, users' emails come back blanked to an empty string while names remain — so a missing email can mean 'shared view', not 'no email on file'.
Team listings fail soft: an empty team list can mean team access is switched off for the group rather than the group genuinely having no teams.
Offboarding a user is irreversible — their private views are hard-deleted and their active sessions are killed, with no restore.
Inviting teammates can partially succeed: some addresses may be sent while others are rejected, and that mixed outcome is reported as a failure rather than a success.
The identity-sync, session-expiry and offboarding operations are service-to-service only (called by the internal identity system); an end-user session or a username + access-key cannot invoke them.

webhook.title: Webhook rule
webhook.description: A stored rule that fires an outbound HTTP request to a target URL when a matching build/test event occurs.
webhook.id_convention: Addressed by the rule's UUID; there is no prefixed display id. Discover the UUID from a list call — it is not the integer database id.

relations.via: project mapping (a group rule links up to 30 projects; a project rule is scoped to one)

key_facts: A webhook rule is addressed by its UUID, which you read from a list call; there is no prefixed display id and it is not the integer database id.
There are two parallel surfaces: project-scoped rules and group-scoped rules that can span many projects. A rule created on one surface is managed on that surface, and the two lists do not overlap.

Listing or reading webhook rules needs no special permission, but creating, editing, toggling, deleting or testing one requires the webhook settings permission — so an account can see rules it is not allowed to change.

Editing a rule replaces its definition in place and keeps no history: an overwritten URL, headers, auth or trigger conditions cannot be recovered. There is no undo short of re-entering the previous values.
Deleting a rule is permanent and also removes its project mappings; disable the rule instead if the intent is only to pause it.
Every create, edit, toggle, delete and test is refused in the demo-sandbox environment.

Testing a rule sends a real outbound HTTP request to the target URL (a server-side call whose side effects land on the target system), and it always reports success even when the target failed — read the isError flag in the body, never the HTTP status, to know if it worked.
A list of rules returns only each rule's summary (name, target URL, event type, enabled flag); the headers, request body and stored auth are returned only when you fetch a single rule by id.
A group rule links at most 30 projects. The 'all projects' scope is available only to Test Management callers; other callers are refused if they try to enter it.
Newly created project-scoped rules are always enabled regardless of the enabled flag sent; use the toggle operation to disable one afterwards.
A rule's target auth can be none, basic (username/password) or bearer token, and the request method is limited to POST or PUT.

ai_insight.title: AI insight (RCA & code-fix)
ai_insight.description: AI-generated root-cause analysis for a failed test run or build, plus the code-fix guidance and session tokens that drive it.
ai_insight.id_convention: No single id. RCA is addressed by the test-run integer id or the build uuid; code-fix preferences by a plain integer id discovered through the get-preference call; RCA conversation turns by a UUID message id.

relations.via: per-test-run RCA and improve-analysis
build-level RCA and RCA chat
code-fix preferences per build name

key_facts: AI features are plan-gated: on a group without the AI test-failure-analysis plan the code-fix and RCA-context calls are refused with 403 PLAN_FEATURE_NOT_ALLOWED, and the session-token call returns empty token and feature list rather than erroring.

Some AI actions also require the calling user to have AI enabled individually, separate from the group plan; the per-user check applies to saving and presigning code-fix guidance but not to deleting it.

Improving (retriggering) an RCA is asynchronous: the call returns a message id and the refreshed analysis is delivered later, so poll the RCA conversation for the result rather than expecting it in the response.

Attaching a file is always a two-step flow: first mint an upload credential, upload the file straight to S3 with it, then quote the returned key when saving a preference or retriggering. The credential step persists nothing on its own.

Uploaded files land in an unconfirmed area and are kept only when a later save or turn submission references their key; an upload that is never referenced is discarded, and there are caps on how many uploads can be pending.
Only agentic RCAs accept extra context uploads; a non-agentic analysis rejects them.
RCA context uploads are refused for test runs older than an allowed age.

Code-fix guidance is keyed by build name within a project, one preference per build name; creating a second for the same build name is refused as already existing, so change it with an update instead.
Deleting code-fix guidance also removes its uploaded files and cannot be undone; the RCA analyses themselves keep no version history.

build.title: Build
build.description: A single CI/automation run reported to Test Observability, grouping the test runs executed together with their aggregate results.
build.id_convention: Addressed by build UUID (an opaque string) on most routes. A few reads take the internal NUMERIC build id instead (e.g. the AI failure summary), and the two are not interchangeable. A build can also be located by its human coordinates (project normalised name + build normalised name + build serial number), which resolve to the UUID. There is no prefixed display identifier.

relations.via: a build contains the test runs executed in it
each build belongs to one project

key_facts: Most build endpoints are keyed by the build UUID, a string. A few instead take the internal numeric build id (the AI failure summary is one), and passing a UUID where a numeric id is expected simply fails to find the build.
A build locked by plan fencing is refused on most insight reads with a plan-feature-not-allowed error even though the build exists; treat that as an entitlement gap, not a missing build.
An unknown build UUID comes back as a build-not-found error on most reads.
Cross-group access is blocked: a build whose owning group does not match the caller reads as not-found on most routes (and as a forbidden error on the coordinate lookups).

A build can be reached by its human coordinates from the dashboard URL (project name + build name + build serial number), which resolve to the UUID; the reverse lookup rebuilds those coordinates from a UUID.
Closing a build cannot be undone through the API — there is no reopen operation — so treat a close as final.

Many insight tiles and history reads accept the same standard build filter set (search text, status, folders, tags, browser/OS, priority, owner, flaky/new-failure/always-failing toggles, and so on); the filter narrows which of the build's tests the metric is computed over.
On demo-sandbox environments some report reads (the authoring report, the optimisation widget) return canned data instead of touching the real backend.
Re-run statistics come in two shapes: a flat legacy summary and a split-build-aware grouped summary; the grouped one is the one to use for split or parent/child builds.

build_filter.title: Build filter
build_filter.description: Filter-option sources for the build listing: the static option catalogue plus per-facet type-ahead value lists.
build_filter.id_convention: Not an addressable record — there is no filter id. A filter view is fetched by scope: one project by its normalised name (a URL-safe slug, discovered from a project read/list), or a set of integer project ids sent in a POST filter body.

relations.via: option values are aggregated from the builds the filter scope resolves to
scoped by project normalised name or project id set

key_facts: Filters are not stored objects you address by id. You fetch either a filter catalogue or a single facet's option list, scoped to one project (by its normalised-name slug) or to a set of project ids passed in a filter body.

Two families exist. A per-project set is scoped by the project's normalised name and searched with a simple prefix. A cross-project 'sidebar' set takes a full build filter body and returns only the option values that actually occur under the currently applied selection across the chosen projects.

The per-project facet lists return option objects that carry separate id, value and label (id is what you send back as the filter selection, label is for display). The cross-project sidebar facet lists return bare values instead (plain strings for branches, build names and tags).

Facet option values come from an Elasticsearch terms aggregation capped at 100 entries, so a facet list is a type-ahead suggestion set, not a guaranteed-complete inventory of every value in the project.

A filter view echoes the caller's currently applied selection back in a resolved 'applied' block (user and team ids turned into names, date range, tags, branches, statuses) alongside a static catalogue of all selectable option lists.

On a freemium workspace some filters are locked behind a paid plan; the build test-filter payload names those locked keys in a separate list rather than dropping them, so a caller can grey them out instead of losing them.
For a split build, the test-filter payload is resolved across the parent build and all of its child legs together, not just the single leg addressed.

The framework filter carries raw values: branded SDK names and pass-through non-SDK values such as 'appium' or 'selenium-4'. Matching is case-insensitive, so send the value exactly as the static catalogue offers it.

dashboard.title: Custom dashboard
dashboard.description: A saved, shareable analytics page of widgets and global filters over test-observability and test-management data.
dashboard.id_convention: UUID (e.g. 07c9f7be-0cd7-4669-8d3d-a1adff0b2aec); discover ids from the dashboard listing — a dashboard name is never accepted in place of the id.

relations.via: widgets

key_facts: A dashboard is addressed by its UUID id; get the id from the dashboard listing first — a dashboard name cannot be used as the identifier.
The dashboard listing and the internal dashboard reads require the Custom Dashboard feature entitlement; without it the listing is refused as feature-inaccessible rather than returning an empty list.
Test Management (TCM) dashboards are hidden from the default listing, which is scoped to Test Observability (source TO); ask for source TCM to see them (or the group must have GCD enabled).
Dashboards keep no version history: an overwritten name, visibility level, widget layout or filter set cannot be restored, and a deleted dashboard is gone permanently along with its widget layout.
A dashboard's visibility level is 1 or 2 and decides whether only the owner or the whole group can see it.
Scheduled reports are stored as dashboards but are excluded from the ordinary dashboard listing; they have their own reports listing, which spans both TO and TCM.

On the public-API write surface a treemap widget's visualization override is silently dropped (not rejected) and widget configs are validated for render-safety up front; the internal write surface does neither.
In demo-sandbox environments the seeded default dashboard cannot be updated or deleted — those calls are rejected with a 400 whose body shape differs from a normal success.

project.title: Project
project.description: A Test Observability container mirroring a TestHub project; groups the builds, runs and dashboards for one app or repo.
project.id_convention: Plain integer project id on most paths; many read/listing paths instead take the project's normalisedName (a URL-safe slug of the project name). A project also carries a separate TestHub project id (thProjectId) used for cross-product linkage. Ids and names are discovered through a project listing.

relations.via: project groups its test plans
project contains its builds

key_facts: A project is addressed two different ways depending on the operation: by its integer id, or by its normalised name (a URL-safe slug of the display name). Carry whichever the capability you picked declares - they are not interchangeable.
Deleting a project is irreversible and cascades in TestHub: every build, run and result under it is removed with it. There is no restore.

A project keeps a separate TestHub project id alongside its own id. Some lookups and the delete path can resolve a TestHub/TCM id to the mirrored observability project, so passing the wrong id family can silently act on a different project.
In the demo-sandbox environment, creating and deleting projects is refused, and the app-bootstrap identity fields (user id and group id) come back null.

Projects are only ever created as a service-to-service mirror of a TestHub project, keyed on the TestHub project id and idempotent on it - there is no customer-facing 'new project' create that a user session can call.
The public project listing is scoped to the caller's group and does not report a total count; it is walked page by page until an empty page is returned.
Automation-coverage figures for a project are computed over all time as an aggregation, not stored on the project, so a read recomputes them and carries the timestamp it was calculated at.

project_setting.title: Project & account settings
project_setting.description: Config for a project or account: build alert rules, failure-category sub-types, auto-close/analyser policies and per-user UI preferences.
project_setting.id_convention: Two conventions in play: the newer settings routes address a project by its normalized NAME (a string slug), the older ones by the numeric observability project id (a plain integer). An alert has a plain integer id (supplied in the body, not the path, when updating). A failure-category sub-type is identified by a string `locator` (and also carries a numeric id). alertTypeId is a plain integer discovered via list_alert_types.

relations.via: every setting is scoped to one project (or, for global/user settings, the account/group)

key_facts: The same project is addressed two ways depending on which generation of the settings surface a capability is on: the newer one takes the project's normalized name (a slug), the older one the numeric project id. Carry whichever the capability you picked declares.

Settings keep no version history. An overwritten alert, sub-type, preference or policy value is gone for good; there is no prior revision to restore. Re-submitting is the only way back, so an edit is reversible only if you kept the old value.

Writes are gated per setting area: managing alerts, failure categories, and general/auto-close policy each need their own project permission. A user who can happily read the settings page may still be refused a write.

Most settings reads are ungated for anyone with project visibility. The exception is the auto-close preview count, which is deliberately locked behind the same permission as changing the policy because it is the heaviest query in the feature.
Global build-type settings are account-wide: excluding a build type hides it from the product's views for every user in the group, not just the caller.
User preferences are per-signed-in-user and span all projects; they are also rewritten per product on the way out, so what a read returns can differ from what was last saved.
A failure-category sub-type carries a short display abbreviation (max 4 characters) as well as a longer name (max 64); its colour must be a hex value.
An auto-close policy that was never set reads as simply disabled, not as a missing record; when enabled it stores a threshold in days plus the epoch second it was turned on.
The list of account-wide excluded build sources comes back empty both when nothing is excluded and when the upstream read failed, so an empty list is not proof that nothing is hidden.

rca_conversation.title: RCA conversation (turn & chat)
rca_conversation.description: One turn of an AI root-cause-analysis chat on a test run or build: a user instruction, the agent's answer, its state and approval.
rca_conversation.id_convention: A turn is addressed by its messageId, a UUID minted server-side (discover it from a create/submit reply or from a conversation list). Build chat threads have their own UUID threadId. The public rcaChat flow instead mints an opaque string turnId (a Redis result key), NOT a messageId — the two id spaces do not interchange.

relations.via: test-level conversations hang off a test run (testRunId / test_run_id)
build-level chat threads and turns hang off a build (buildUUID)

key_facts: There are two separate conversation surfaces: a test-run RCA conversation (the Improve-Analysis panel on one failed test) and a build-level RCA chat (a multi-thread assistant on a whole build). They share the turn shape but not their storage, ids, or lifecycle.

Every turn is asynchronous. Submitting or retrying a turn returns immediately with the turn accepted, NOT answered — the answer arrives later. Poll the single-turn read until the turn's state leaves PENDING (PENDING/WORKFLOW_PENDING mean still working; COMPLETED/FAILED are terminal).
Turns are append-only. There is no regenerate operation — to get a fresh answer, submit a new turn with the same instruction; it gets a new turn id and the old turn is left in place.
Approving a turn OVERWRITES the test run's stored RCA with that turn's analysis. The previous analysis is replaced, not versioned, and there is no undo.
Discarding a turn only records a rejection on that turn; the test run keeps whatever RCA it already had.
A turn can be approved or discarded only once, and only after it has reached COMPLETED. A second decision on the same turn, or a decision on a still-running turn, is refused.
On a test run the web Improve-Analysis flow and the MCP agent flow are mutually exclusive: whichever posts first owns the run. Approving is refused when the run's RCA is owned by the MCP agent.

The build chat is organised into threads, each scoped to one user: a caller only ever sees their own threads and their own turns, and there is a per-user active-thread cap (default 10) that create-thread and the first turn of a lazy-created thread both enforce.

The public rcaChat turn result lives in a short-lived store with a TTL. A turn is pollable only while its result survives; after it expires, or if the id belongs to another group's test run, the poll reports the turn as not found rather than erroring.

A turn's metadata is sanitised on read: only the agent's thinking data and the user's approval decision are exposed. Model name, provider, token counts, cost and raw failure class are stripped and never returned.

Two of the build endpoints (the agent completion callback and the workflow-event callback) are service-to-service only, authenticated with a service API key; a normal user token is rejected and they are not part of the customer-facing surface.

sp_test.title: Suite Health test (Stability & Performance)
sp_test.description: A unique automated test tracked across runs in Suite Health, keyed by a stability hash, carrying stability, failure and duration metrics.
sp_test.id_convention: Identified by an opaque stabilityHash string, not a numeric id. The hash is discovered from the Suite Health test listing; the same hash addresses every Test Health detail read.

relations.via: aggregated over the test's executions across builds

key_facts: A test is identified by an opaque stabilityHash string, not a numeric id. You must discover the hash from the Suite Health test listing first; the same hash is what every Test Health detail read takes.
Every Suite Health read is scoped to a date window, and a two-element millisecond [from, to] range is mandatory: results only ever cover that window, and omitting the range is rejected.
The filter type-ahead suggestions are capped server-side and are suggestions, not the complete set: git branches cap at ~100, while build tags, test tags and host names cap at ~10.

Metric counts for the very same query can differ depending on an account feature flag: with the new build listing enabled and the query not restricted to automation-latest, failure counts are sourced from workflow status rather than the raw recorded status, so the same window can report different failure numbers.
Muted-test visibility is an explicit, required input on the Test Health detail reads (show all, only muted, or only unmuted) with no default value.
Suite Health metrics and the environment breakdown exclude archived builds.

The Suite Health filter sidebar degrades gracefully: run-level dropdown options are fetched from an upstream service under a timeout, and on timeout those specific dropdowns come back empty instead of failing the whole request.

test_detail.title: Test detail (logs, hooks, capabilities)
test_detail.description: The logs, hooks, capabilities and error detail attached to one test run, shown on the Test Details page.
test_detail.id_convention: Not its own id. Most tabs are addressed by the parent test run's INTEGER id (testRunId); session-scoped log tabs by the session's HASHED string id; the app-log stream by the test run's UUID. Discover these from a test-run / session read.

relations.via: detail of a test run
session hashed id

key_facts: The detail is derived, not stored as its own record: it has no id of its own and no history to restore. Everything here is read-only and nothing mutates the run.

The same detail is addressed three different ways depending on the tab: most tabs by the test run's integer id, the session-scoped log tabs by the session's hashed string id, and the application-log stream by the test run's UUID. Carry whichever id the capability you picked declares.

Log tabs come in two flavours. One downloads and merges the log text server-side and returns it inline; the other returns only URLs for the caller to fetch. The inline-merge form is slow for long sessions, so prefer the URL form there.

Application logs are filtered to abnormal (error-level) lines only, capped at 5000 lines, and bounded to the run's own start/finish window (padded five seconds each side). A clean run legitimately returns an empty list.
Retention-locked or plan-locked builds refuse every detail read with a forbidden / plan-feature-not-allowed error rather than returning empty; treat that as a plan gap, not a missing run.

Hook attribution is heuristic: hooks are matched by same build, filename, OS, browser and device, latest run only. It is not a stored parent/child link, so hooks from a differently-configured session never appear.
On the demo-sandbox environment several of these reads return canned or empty payloads (an empty log envelope, a demo HAR, or logs chosen by test name) instead of real data.

test_run.title: Test run
test_run.description: One execution of a single test within a build — its status, platform, code, retries and failure analysis.
test_run.id_convention: Most routes take the INTEGER test run id (Long). A few public routes are scoped by the parent BUILD's UUID instead (a string). Discover run ids from a build's test-run listing rather than guessing them; the TR-NNN prefixed identifier some surfaces show is for display, not for these numeric paths.

relations.via: buildId
groups

key_facts: A test run is found by its own numeric id and the caller's group; when a route's path also carries a build id, some routes use it and some ignore it entirely, so a run still resolves even if the build segment is wrong.

The baseline, similar-error and hooks reads return a MAP keyed by test run id, not a single object, and the map is EMPTY (not an error) when nothing qualifies — an empty body means 'none found', not a failure.
The baseline look-back is a fixed 30 days before the run's start time; a last-known-good run older than that is invisible, so a returned empty map does not prove the test never passed.
Downloading a run's attachments or screenshots is gated by an account feature; when it is off the attachment read is refused even for a run that clearly has attachments.
Attachment and screenshot downloads come back as presigned URLs that expire roughly two hours after they are issued — fetch them promptly and re-request rather than caching the URL.
A test can be muted with an automatic unmute condition (after N passes, or after a date); making that mute permanent is reversible by muting again with a condition, so it is a change, not a deletion.
The bug-report read composes a fresh, pre-filled ticket draft from the failure; it does NOT fetch a bug that was already filed.
Linking a filed bug to a run is idempotent on the issue key: linking the same key twice is a silent no-op, and the link can be removed again afterwards.
Retries of a test are separate executions, each with its own status; a run carries its retry history rather than overwriting the previous attempt.

Public listings are plan- and source-aware: a freemium or source-fenced build yields a stripped or empty result rather than the analysis fields, and smart-tag filters on such a build are refused outright.
The status a run reports is lowercased on the public /ext detail routes but may come back uppercase from other surfaces — compare case-insensitively.
In the flat build listing the top-level id of each row is the test's hash (a string), while the numeric run id lives under that row's details.id.

ai_failure.title: AI failure analysis (build-level)
ai_failure.description: A build-level AI cluster of related test failures: a failure theme or a workflow grouping the runs that failed for the same reason.
ai_failure.id_convention: The build is addressed by its build UUID (an opaque string) in the path. Individual clusters are identified by an integer buildFailureThemeId or buildFailureWorkflowId, which are discovered from the build AI-failures read, not guessable.

relations.via: buildUUID
flat test-run drill-down under a theme/workflow

key_facts: AI failure clustering is computed asynchronously. Requesting analysis on a build that has none returns immediately with a triggered flag and NO themes or workflows yet; the results arrive later, so re-read to collect them.
The read side returns only what has already been computed and never starts analysis. Starting analysis is a separate trigger operation.
Themes and workflows always come back sorted by their share of failures, highest first.

Build-level AI analysis is gated by AI opt-in consent, a per-account AI-enabled flag, and the build-level RCA feature; a trial account also has a usage quota that returns a plan-not-allowed error once exhausted, and each fresh trigger consumes one unit of it.
A build whose source is excluded by source-fencing is refused analysis.
The trial-quota figure is present only for accounts on the build-level AI trial; a paid account never sees it, so its absence does not mean zero usage.
Drilling from a cluster to its test runs is cursor-paginated, and the per-page size is a fixed backend default that the caller cannot change.

session.title: Session
session.description: A single automation run on BrowserStack (Automate or App Automate) recorded against a build, with its config, timings, logs and status.
session.id_convention: Most session reads take the session's hashed id, an opaque alphanumeric string (not a numeric id). The stop control takes that hashed id in the body. One list read is the exception: it takes the NUMERIC build id even though its slot looks like a session id.

relations.via: buildId
a session executes the build's test runs

key_facts: A session is identified by its hashed id (a string), not a numeric id, except the per-build session list, which takes the build's numeric id even though the value slots where the other routes expect a session id.
App profiling exists only for App Automate sessions; asking for it on an Automate session is rejected, and an empty object means the report is still generating or was never captured, not an error.
Session detail can come back with a retryable not-ready status while the session is still being linked to its build; treat that as retry-shortly, not a failure.
A session that belongs to a plan-locked build is refused with a plan-not-allowed error even though the session exists.
A public-link viewer does not see still-running sessions in the per-build session list.
Stopping a session ends the live run and cannot be undone, but removes nothing: the session record and its logs remain.
The public test-code read reports a session that exists but captured no code identically to a missing session, so a not-found there does not prove the id is wrong.
On the demo sandbox environment, capabilities, session details and app profiling are served from a canned dataset rather than real data.

check_config.title: Check configuration (SCM check-run)
check_config.description: A repo's SCM check-run rule: which BrowserStack build/project a commit or PR check reports on, as quality-gate or build status.
check_config.id_convention: Check-configuration id is a plain integer (discover it from the repo's check-runs listing). A checks-mapping registration has its OWN integer ingestion id, which is neither the check-configuration id nor the GitHub check id.
key_facts: The whole feature is gated by the CHECKS_EVALUATION entitlement: create, read, list, update, delete and toggle all refuse when the workspace lacks it, and that refusal is flattened into a generic bad-request error rather than a typed one.

Check configurations are scoped to the caller's group AND user together: you only see and can change checks you created, and a teammate's checks are invisible and cannot be edited, toggled or deleted.
A repository may hold at most 10 check configurations; a configuration is unique by the combination of its name, repository, group, build name and target project.
checkType is one of exactly two values: quality-gate status or build status.
The target project named on a check must already exist in the workspace, or the write is refused as project-not-found.
Deleting a check configuration removes the row for good; there is no undo and no bin.

A checks-mapping registration is a separate record from the check configuration it points at: it captures one pull request's commit, callback URL and evaluation state (starting at 'Not Started'), and is addressed by its own ingestion id.

A checks-mapping registration only succeeds for check ids that already match an existing check configuration in the caller's group for that repository and organisation; ids that match nothing are rejected.

view.title: Saved view
view.description: A named saved filter preset for a listing screen, private to its creator or shared with the whole group.
view.id_convention: A view id is a UUID (discover it from a views listing). The path viewType is a SCREEN name, not an id: one of builds, testRuns, testHealth, uniqueErrors or buildInsights.
key_facts: A view belongs to exactly one screen type (builds, test runs, test health, unique errors or build insights); the same name can be reused across different screen types.
Views are either private (level 1, visible only to the creator) or shared/public (level 2, visible to the whole group).
A view name must be unique within its screen type: within the group for shared views, within the creator for private views. A clash is refused with a name-exists error rather than overwriting.
Deleting a view is a hard, unrecoverable removal, and the view disappears from every group member's view switcher immediately.
The creator and group of a view are always taken from the caller's session, never from the request body; a createdBy or groupId sent in the body is ignored.
On a shared public link only public views are returned; private views are never exposed through a shared link.
Editing a view is a partial update (omitted fields keep their stored values), but views keep no revision history, so an overwritten name, filter query or visibility cannot be restored.

The external (public-API) surface enforces stricter input than the internal one: name must be non-blank and at most 100 characters, query non-blank and at most 4000, and it has no delete operation at all.

dashboard_view.title: Dashboard view
dashboard_view.description: A saved dashboard configuration (name, global filters, widget layout) for the Test Observability or Test Management dashboard page.
dashboard_view.id_convention: UUID. Custom views' UUIDs are discovered from the list capability. On READS only, three built-in views are also addressable by alias: `default` resolves to the TCM view for source=TCM and to the TO 'testing trends' view for source=TO, and `automation-trend` resolves to the automation-trend view. Writes (update/delete/clone-source) require the raw UUID; the aliases are rejected there.
key_facts: There are three built-in dashboards: the default TCM dashboard, the default TO dashboard (shown as 'testing trends'), and 'automation-trend'. None of the three can be renamed, edited, cloned into, or deleted; an attempt to update or delete one is refused, and the built-ins never appear as normal editable views.

A dashboard is addressed by its UUID everywhere. Only when reading a single dashboard may you also use the aliases `default` and `automation-trend` in place of the UUID; every write needs the raw UUID.
Opening a built-in default dashboard forces its date range to the last 30 days, ignoring whatever range was stored, and injects the current filter values into its widgets.

Reading a single dashboard records it in your 'recently viewed' dashboards list (the same list the home page shows); there is no read that avoids leaving that trace. The trace is skipped for super-users unless they are in group 2.
Dashboards keep no version history: an overwritten name, filter set, or widget layout cannot be restored to a previous revision, and a delete is permanent.
Dashboard names must be unique within the project; creating or cloning with a name already in use is rejected.

Every operation on this entity must name a project (by id, name, or identifier). The named project both scopes the dashboard and is the resource the create/update/delete/clone permission check runs against, even for calls that otherwise ignore the project.
Visibility is governed by the numeric `level` field on the dashboard; the default level is 2 (group / shared).
Custom (private/group) dashboards are only visible to their owner and their group; a UUID that belongs to someone else's private dashboard reads as not-found rather than forbidden.
A dashboard name is limited to 1-100 characters.

redaction_rule.title: Log-redaction & pattern rule
redaction_rule.description: A project's regex rule that masks matching text out of ingested test logs (also groups failure-pattern rules).
redaction_rule.id_convention: Log-redaction rules use a plain integer id (ruleId), returned by the list/create calls — discover it from the list, never guess. Failure-pattern rules also use a plain integer id, discovered from the pattern-rules list. Pattern-analysis settings have no id.

relations.via: a failure-pattern rule's issueType is an issue-type locator

key_facts: Every project is addressed by its normalised name, not a numeric id, on the log-redaction and pattern-rule settings; a project outside the caller's group is treated as not found.
A project may hold at most 10 log-redaction rules; creating an 11th is rejected.

A redaction (or failure-pattern, or standalone-validated) pattern must be a valid RE2J regex — Google RE2, not Java's regex — so backreferences and lookaround are rejected even though they are valid Java syntax.
A redaction pattern may be up to 1024 characters, but the standalone regex validator caps patterns at only 64 characters — a much shorter limit for the same syntax.
A redaction pattern must be unique within the project; adding one that already exists is rejected.
Redaction applies only to logs ingested AFTER the change — existing logs are never re-scanned, and because the original text is never stored, a redaction cannot be undone on logs already masked.
Matched text is replaced with the literal string [MASKED].
Redaction rules run in priority order (lowest priorityOrder first); reordering changes which rule masks a given line first but does not change what is masked overall.

A redaction change reaches the ingestion pipeline with a small lag — it is mirrored to a shared cache only after the database change commits — so a just-saved rule may not affect the very next log line immediately.
Turning a redaction rule off leaves it stored but stops it masking; once no enabled rule remains, the whole project stops being redacted.
Failure-pattern rules are a separate, plan-gated feature: without the pattern-analysis entitlement every create, update and delete of a failure-pattern rule is refused, though the list still returns.
Failure-pattern rules are also capped at 10 per project and live in the TestHub backend, so they are edited through a pass-through rather than stored alongside redaction rules.
A failure-pattern rule maps matches to an issue type given as a locator string (not a numeric id); a locator the project does not have is rejected.
Deleting a rule of either kind is permanent — there is no version history or restore, and already-applied categorisations from a deleted failure-pattern rule are not reverted.

Pattern-analysis settings and pattern-analysis (failure-pattern) rules are distinct: the settings toggle whether failure patterns are detected at all, while the rules define individual match-to-category mappings.

repo_setting.title: Repo setting (AI tag configuration)
repo_setting.description: A per-project link between a build name and one or more source repositories, used to generate AI test tags from that repo's code.
repo_setting.id_convention: Plain integer id (the `id` field). It is NOT the build name — discover a configuration's id from the list call before addressing it.

relations.via: scoped by projectName in the path

key_facts: A repo configuration links one build name to one or more source-repository entries; the AI test tags for that build are generated from the linked repository's code.

The integer `id` addresses a configuration everywhere. The build name is a separate lookup key — one read fetches a configuration by its build name, but edit, delete, generation and tag reads all take the integer id, which you get from the list.

Creating a configuration does NOT immediately register it with the downstream code-tag service; the link only reaches that service on the first tag-generation request. A status or tag read taken before generating tags can therefore report that nothing exists yet.
Tag generation is asynchronous. Starting it returns the downstream service's acknowledgement, and progress is observed by polling the generation status separately, not from the trigger response.
The generation status cannot distinguish 'never started' from 'nothing to report yet' — before any run has been registered it comes back as an empty result rather than an error.

Editing a configuration is a full replace, not a patch: both the build name and at least one repository entry must be supplied every time, and there is no version history, so overwritten repository details cannot be recovered.

Deleting a configuration removes the local link and pushes a single, no-retry removal to the downstream code-tag service; if that downstream removal fails the local link is restored and the call errors, so a failed delete leaves everything as it was.

Creating, editing, deleting and generating tags all require the account's per-user AI feature to be enabled, and are refused when AI is turned off; plain reads of a configuration are not gated that way.

Smart-tag settings are a distinct project-level configuration on this same surface: the flaky / always-failing / new-failure / performance-anomaly thresholds that decide how tests are automatically labelled. They are rule-based labels, unrelated to the AI tags generated from a source repository.
Changing smart-tag settings is reversible by setting them again, but no prior-value history is kept.

For the flaky 'flake in history' rule the flipping count must be strictly less than the consecutive-run window; an equal or larger flipping count is rejected before the change is even permission-checked, so this validation error can surface even for a caller who lacks edit permission.

report.title: Report (saved report)
report.description: A saved, shareable analytics view over test runs with persisted global filters and widgets; private or group-visible.
report.id_convention: UUID (the report id). Reports mirrored from Test Management are ALSO addressable by their TM-side numeric external report id through the sync surface. Discover a report's UUID from the report listing.

relations.via: selected projects in the report's global filters
the tabular test-runs report widget

key_facts: Reports and dashboards are the same stored object under the hood and share one storage, name space and permission family; a report is just the report-typed view of it, so its visibility, filters and widgets behave exactly like a dashboard's.
A report is addressed two ways for the same record: end-user reports by a UUID, and reports mirrored from Test Management additionally by their TM-side numeric external id on the sync surface.

Visibility level is 1 = private (only the owner sees it) or 2 = group (everyone in the group sees it). A report you own at any level, or any group-level (level 2) report in your group, is yours to delete.
Report names must be unique within the same type and visibility level; a clashing name is rejected on create, on clone, and on an edit that changes the name, type or level.
Reports keep no version history — a rename, filter change or widget replacement overwrites the previous definition with no way to restore it.

A report stores its columns and filters by numeric custom-field id, so rendering or editing a saved report means resolving those ids back to display names first; the same field name can exist at both the test-case and test-execution level, distinguished only by entity type.
Only the tabular test-runs report type has live data behind it; asking a report's tiles or dataset for any other report type returns a 200 with a null body rather than an error.

Reports mirrored from Test Management are stamped with a TCM source and are meant to be written only by the Test Management service (identity taken from the request body, no permission check); the end-user builder creates reports under the TO source.
In the demo-sandbox environment there is a built-in default report that cannot be edited or deleted.

Creating or listing reports requires the custom-dashboard plan feature, and minting a report's PDF-print token requires the download-report plan feature; without the feature the call is refused even for a user who holds report permissions.

report_view.title: Report view
report_view.description: A configured analytics report (currently the tabular test-runs report) run on demand to return its table, summary tiles and per-test detail.
report_view.id_convention: No stored id: the report is defined by the definition sent in the request body. Per-test detail is keyed by a test's globalTestHash (a string hash identifying one test case across runs), taken from a report-table row.

relations.via: report rows / per-test detail

key_facts: Only the tabular test-runs report is implemented. Asking for any other report type returns an empty or null body with a 200, not an error, so check the body rather than the status.
The report is defined entirely by the definition you send (datasets, segments, global filters); the id in the address is not read at all, so any value satisfies it.
Running the report has no side effects even though the request is write-shaped: the body is the query, not saved state.
The report table and its summary tiles are two separate calls that take the same definition; the tiles call has no paging.
Per-test detail (stats, run list, trend) is keyed by a test's global hash, which you read from a row of the report table.
A test with no matching runs in the window returns an empty object for its stats rather than zeroed counts.
Trend point durations are in milliseconds, and each point carries the build it came from.
When every dataset in the definition mutually conflicts, the table comes back empty and the tiles come back with all zero/false fencing flags rather than an error.

widget.title: Dashboard widget
widget.description: A single configured tile on a dashboard (chart, stat card or distribution) whose data is computed on demand from filters and a time window.
widget.id_convention: Addressed on these routes by a widget-type enum plus the definition in the body, not by a stored widget id. The dashboard id in the address is not read on the data and drill-down calls.

relations.via: dashboardId (unused on data routes)

key_facts: Widget data is computed from the definition and filters you send, not read from stored widget state; the dashboard id in the address is ignored on the org-level data and drill-down calls.
Filter-value lookups come in two forms: a flat list of values for one filter key, and an enhanced form that splits values into suggested and others with search and paging.
For ClickHouse-powered widget types, the project ids you send are automatically translated to TestHub project ids before the query runs.
Group 2 asking for the active-builds widget is forced to a seven-day window regardless of the range requested.
These reads have no side effects even though the requests are write-shaped.
The widget-data response shape depends on the widget type requested, so read the type you asked for before assuming a chart vs card vs distribution envelope.

parallel_queue.title: Parallel queue usage
parallel_queue.description: A view of a group's parallel-session concurrency for a product: parallels in use vs allowed and queued sessions vs the queue limit.
parallel_queue.id_convention: Scoped to the authenticated caller's group; the running-builds view additionally takes a numeric user id in the address.
key_facts: Usage is always for the signed-in caller's group and the product named in the request (automate or app-automate). A product value other than automate is treated as app-automate on the running-builds view.
The team breakdown and running-builds views pass through to the billing backend using the caller's own BrowserStack credentials, so an unrecognised product fails downstream there.

The summary view only works for session/JWT callers because it reads the user from the security context; omit the product and you get back only the test-execution usage block, with no live queue numbers.
The running-builds view takes a user id in the address and does not check that it belongs to the caller's own group.
The summary view strips the internal user-details block out before returning.

usage.title: Usage & entitlement
usage.description: Test-execution consumption and plan/tier entitlement for a group or user: counts run, limits, and how much of the plan is used.
usage.id_convention: Group/user scoping comes from query params or the authenticated session; the device-tier and plan-details views use the caller's own group with no id argument.
key_facts: The raw execution-count view takes the user id or group id straight from the request and never checks they belong to the caller, so any authenticated caller can read another user's or group's counts.
That same count view returns a 200 with the plain text body 'Missing userId or groupId' when both are omitted, instead of a 400.
The plan/usage-details view returns every count as a compacted display string (e.g. '1.2K'), not a number, and nulls out every usage field when the group has no execution limit configured.
The device-tier view lists only mobile tiers; non-mobile tiers are filtered out, and a missing product is a 400.
Execution counts are split into all tests reported and the subset that ran on BrowserStack infrastructure (those carrying a session id).

report_share.title: Report share by email
report_share.description: Sharing a report link by email, which also invites any not-yet-registered recipients into the BrowserStack group.
report_share.id_convention: No stored id; the report being shared is identified by the link URL carried in the request.

relations.via: shared link

key_facts: Sharing has two side effects, not one: it emails the report link and it creates group invitations for any recipients who are not already in the group.
The link's host must end in browserstack.com (or the staging domain in non-production) or the whole request is rejected as an invalid link; a link string with no host skips that check.
Recipients are split into new users (invited, then emailed) and existing users (emailed only); sending neither list is rejected as empty.
In the demo-sandbox environment the call returns a canned response and sends nothing.
When inviting fails the call returns an error body rather than raising, so read the success flag instead of relying on the status.

search.title: Global search
search.description: A global free-text search across product entities (builds, tests, projects) for the search bar and quick overlay.
search.id_convention: No stored entity; each result carries its own numeric id and a type discriminator.
key_facts: Search covers a fixed set of entity types and rejects any other value; the accepted values are case-sensitive (Build, BuildTestCaseExecutionResult, Project, All).
The query must be at least three characters and not blank, or the request is rejected.
Results are always sorted by most-recently-updated; the sort order cannot be changed by the caller.
The quick-overlay mode returns a smaller page and omits the paging and total-count fields that the full mode includes.
Each result is enriched with the matching record's user name, resolved from its user id.

self_healing.title: Self-healing (AI-healed locators)
self_healing.description: AI-suggested replacement selectors for tests whose locators broke, plus the review verdicts and PRs that apply them.
self_healing.id_convention: A build is addressed by its build UUID (^[a-zA-Z0-9-]{1,64}$). A healing-PR job is a random UUID (8-4-4-4-12 hex) returned by create_self_healing_pr; it is NOT discoverable through any list call and lives only in Redis with a short TTL, so capture it from the create response.

relations.via: healed locators are computed per build; summary and verdicts are build-scoped
each healed selector carries the sessionId of the run it broke in

key_facts: Opening a healing PR is asynchronous: the create call returns immediately with a job id and an IN_PROGRESS state, and the actual GitHub PR is opened later by a background worker. Poll the status separately; the PR URL only appears once the job reaches a terminal state.
A healing-PR job's terminal state can be SUCCEEDED, PARTIAL (some files changed, some skipped), FAILED, or NO_CHANGES_NEEDED. PARTIAL and NO_CHANGES_NEEDED are successful outcomes, not errors.

Healing-PR job state is kept only briefly and only for the group that started it; once it expires the id reads as not-found rather than as a finished state, so a job whose status was never polled in time is unrecoverable.

Opening a healing PR is GitHub-only and needs the build to carry version-control info (origin remote, branch) and the group to have a GitHub source-code integration connected; a GitHub Enterprise or non-standard host must pass an explicit owner/repo.

The human-in-the-loop verdict flow (recording whether a healed locator was accurate) is an optional feature per group. When it is off, reading verdicts returns an empty list while submitting a verdict is refused outright.
Only reviewers with a full product role can record a verdict; view-only members cannot.

A recorded verdict can carry over from an earlier build: a build shows verdicts first captured against a previous build, flagged as carryover, so the same healed element is not re-reviewed every build.
Self-heal summary numbers require the build to be within the account's plan quota; a build locked by quota is refused rather than returning zeroes.

The healing report itself (the list of individual healed selectors, with their original and healed values) is delivered as a downloadable report artefact, separate from these APIs; the summary here is only the headline counts.

build_comparison.title: Build comparison
build_comparison.description: A side-by-side diff of two builds (a base and a target) showing which tests newly failed, started passing, were added or dropped.
build_comparison.id_convention: Not a stored entity with its own id: a comparison is identified by the pair of build UUIDs passed as the `base` and `target` query params. Comparison is always done at the top-level parent build, so a re-run/child UUID should be normalised first via resolve_build_comparison_parent_uuids.

relations.via: base and target are both build UUIDs

key_facts: Every comparison endpoint takes exactly two required query params, `base` and `target`, each a build UUID; an empty or missing one comes back as build-not-found.

Comparison is defined only between two top-level parent builds. Child builds, archived builds and plan-locked builds are rejected as unsupported, so normalise a pasted re-run UUID to its parent before comparing.

The two builds must come from compatible sources. An incompatible pair is not an error: the response comes back with source-fencing flags set and its actual comparison payload empty, so check for those flags before trusting empty counts.

Comparing is a paid feature: the aggregation, the per-bucket listing and the availability pre-check are all refused when the plan does not include build comparison. Resolving parent UUIDs and fetching the two build headers are NOT plan-gated and work regardless.

The side-by-side header counts are recomputed with the same de-duplication the comparison buckets use, so the header agrees with the buckets; this makes the header fetch heavier than a plain build summary and it silently falls back to raw counts if that recompute fails.

The whole flow is heavy: it resolves both builds' child builds and runs search + aggregation across them, with a large per-build ceiling on the test rows it will pull, so treat these as expensive reads.
A typical page flow is: normalise both UUIDs to parents, check the pair is comparable, fetch the two headers and the headline counts, then drill into one bucket's tests.

comment.title: Comment
comment.description: A rich-text note left on a build, test run or test, threaded and able to @mention group users, used for review discussion.
comment.id_convention: A comment id is a random UUID string generated on create and returned in the create response. A comment belongs to a thread identified by threadId (also a UUID; a new top-level comment starts its own thread). There is no list-by-id call: ids are discovered through the build/test comment reads.

relations.via: buildUuid / buildSerialId
runUuid / testHash
scoped by project normalised name in the path

key_facts: Comments are a paid feature: creating, editing and deleting are refused when the plan does not include comments.
A comment can only be edited or deleted by the person who wrote it; another user's comment reads as not-found on those operations even inside the same group.
Comments have no version history. Editing a comment overwrites its body in place with no way to recover the previous text.
Reads are bounded by the plan's data-retention window, so older comments silently fall out of results rather than erroring.
@mentioning a group user notifies them shortly after the comment is posted; the notification is a side effect that fires even though the create call has already returned.
Comment reads are keyed to a build's numeric serial id and look back over a fixed window of preceding builds (so recurring discussion on the same test carries across re-runs), not over all history.
The public /ext read is view-only: there is no external endpoint to post a comment, only the group-authenticated internal ones can create.

sp_error.title: Unique error (Suite Health)
sp_error.description: A cluster of test failures sharing one error signature in a project, the unit of the Suite Health Unique Errors view.
sp_error.id_convention: Numeric cluster id (errorClusterId), a plain integer discovered from the unique-errors list (each row's `id`, returned as a numeric string). Every detail view takes it in the path as errorId / clusterId.

relations.via: impacted tests hitting the error (breakdown / platforms)
builds in which the error occurred (details/builds)

key_facts: A cluster id is a plain integer. Get it from the unique-errors list (each row's `id`, a numeric string); every per-error detail view takes that same value in its path.
Every Unique Errors call needs a date window of EXACTLY two epoch-millisecond bounds; omitting it or sending one bound is rejected. A single lowerBound/upperBound pair is the only fallback.

These views only ever consider FAILED test runs. Archived builds and usage-locked builds are always excluded, and manual (Test Management) runs are excluded from the list and per-error queries whatever you send.
On a demo tenant, or a real project that has no builds yet, the list answers with an empty set and a success status, not a not-found. Only a genuinely absent project is a 404.
Free / non-pro accounts are capped: the list returns only the single highest-occurrence error and is force-sorted by occurrence count descending, and per-error filtering is skipped.

Source feature-fencing can silently drop Automate, App-Automate or low-code tests from results; the list response carries automateTestsSkipped / appAutomateTestsSkipped / lcncTestsSkipped booleans that say when this happened.
The window is clamped to the account's data-retention range before querying, so a range wider than retention silently returns only the retained slice.
Every Unique Errors endpoint is read-only and accepts central-auth, obs token, service key, rails-basic, public-link and speedboat tokens; none of them accepts username + access-key auth.
Occurrence bar/chart data comes back as bare per-bucket counts with no timestamps on some views, so the time axis has to be reconstructed from the requested window; buckets are one calendar day.

test_rca.title: Test RCA (AI root-cause analysis)
test_rca.description: The AI root-cause analysis stored for a single failed test run, with its generation state and thinking data.
test_rca.id_convention: No id of its own in paths: an RCA is addressed by the integer test-run id it belongs to (one RCA per test run). The stored row does carry an integer id and a bulkRcaId (UUID) linking runs analysed together in one bulk request.

relations.via: one RCA per test run, keyed by test run id

key_facts: Generating an RCA is asynchronous: a request only queues the work, and the finished analysis arrives later. The immediate reply carries a state field, not the completed analysis; the terminal states are Completed (success) and the error states (LLM_SERVICE_ERROR, LOG_FETCH_ERROR, AI_SYSTEM_ERROR, UNKNOWN_ERROR, TIMEOUT).
